name: Tasman Peninsula
tagline: Convict ruins and Australia's highest sea cliffs, an easy run from Hobart.
description: The Tasman Peninsula hangs off Tasmania's south-east, joined to the mainland by the narrow isthmus at Eaglehawk Neck. It was the centre of convict transportation, and the Port Arthur penitentiary and the Coal Mines are World Heritage-listed parts of the Australian Convict Sites. The coast is just as big a draw, with dolerite capes, sea arches, caves and a blowhole along the cliffs, which are Australia's highest. Port Arthur, Nubeena and Eaglehawk Neck are the main places to base, within reach of Hobart.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass and Three Capes booking
goodToKnow.detail: Entering a national park on the peninsula needs a valid Tasmanian parks pass, and bookings are essential for the Three Capes Track.

goodToKnow.title: A car is the way around
goodToKnow.detail: The Arthur Highway runs most of the region's length, and there are few buses and no taxi service, so a car is the practical way to get around.

goodToKnow.title: Weather can change
goodToKnow.detail: Conditions in Tasmania can change at any time of year, so check the forecast, plan for poor weather and stay within barriers at cliff edges.

name: Freycinet
tagline: Pink granite peaks above the crescent of Wineglass Bay on Tasmania's east coast.
description: Freycinet National Park covers the Freycinet Peninsula on the east coast, where the pink granite peaks of the Hazards rise above azure bays and white sand beaches. It was founded in 1916, making it one of Tasmania's two oldest parks. Wineglass Bay is the headline view, but the park also has the Friendly Beaches, a lighthouse boardwalk at Cape Tourville and granite summits. Coles Bay is the settlement beside the park, and Swansea is the largest nearby town.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass required
goodToKnow.detail: A valid Tasmanian parks pass is needed to enter, and a pass for a vehicle covers up to eight occupants.

goodToKnow.title: Tracks are steep and rocky
goodToKnow.detail: Walks often cross steep granite and loose gravel, so wear sturdy shoes; Mount Amos is a Grade 4 climb over rock slabs that are dangerous when wet.

goodToKnow.title: Drive carefully at dusk
goodToKnow.detail: Wallabies and wombats are on the roads from dusk to dawn, and an advisory 60 km/h limit applies near the park after dark.

name: Bicheno
tagline: A small east-coast town with a blowhole, wildlife and penguins after dark.
description: Bicheno is a small coastal town on the Tasman Highway, known for its colony of little penguins and as a base for Freycinet National Park. A waterfront track links the Gulch harbour, the blowhole and Diamond Island. Inland, Douglas-Apsley National Park has dry forest, gorges and swimming waterholes. Penguin tours run at night, and numbers are highest in summer.

goodToKnow.title: Book penguin tours ahead
goodToKnow.detail: Penguin tours run nightly and the numbers are limited, so book ahead in summer; there are almost none ashore in winter.

goodToKnow.title: The blowhole is unfenced
goodToKnow.detail: Waves can crash right over it in big seas, so stay well back from the edge, especially in storms and high tides.

goodToKnow.title: Penguins on the road
goodToKnow.detail: Take care driving after dark, particularly on the Tasman Highway near the Diamond Island end of town.

name: Launceston
tagline: Tasmania's second city, with a gorge 1 km from the centre.
description: Launceston was settled in 1805 and is Tasmania's second-largest city and the main base for northern Tasmania. It has a museum and art gallery and a brewery that runs tours. Cataract Gorge, 1 km from the centre, has walking tracks, a swimming pool and a chairlift across the gorge. Brickendon, a working farm at Longford founded in 1824 and part of the Australian Convict Sites, and the Tamar Valley are nearby.

whyVisitSubjects: Cataract Gorge and its suspension bridge

goodToKnow.title: Gorge parking is paid
goodToKnow.detail: Parking at the gorge entrance is paid, by the hour or all day, but walking in and swimming are free.

goodToKnow.title: A car helps
goodToKnow.detail: A car is the easiest way around, though the city also has a Metro bus service and a cycle path network runs out towards the gorge.

goodToKnow.title: Swim with care
goodToKnow.detail: The gorge water is cold with a current, so use the constructed entrances or the free, unheated pool.

name: Tamar Valley
tagline: Wine, wildlife and a river-mouth lighthouse along the Tamar.
description: The Tamar Valley runs north from Launceston along the Tamar River to Bass Strait, and is Tasmania's largest wine region, with over 30 cellar doors along its wine trail. The east bank is known for sparkling wines and the west bank for pinot noir. Beauty Point has a platypus house and a seahorse farm, and Low Head Lighthouse, built in 1833, stands at the river mouth. The heritage centre at Beaconsfield recalls the gold mine and the 2006 rescue of two trapped miners.

goodToKnow.title: Pick a driver
goodToKnow.detail: Cellar doors are spread along both banks, so allow a day, choose a designated driver and follow the wine trail.

goodToKnow.title: Drive the valley
goodToKnow.detail: The valley runs from Launceston to Bass Strait, and a car is the practical way to link the towns, cellar doors and lookouts.

name: Bay of Fires
tagline: White beaches and orange lichen-covered granite on the north-east coast.
description: The Bay of Fires is a run of white beaches, clear blue water and orange granite boulders on Tasmania's north-east coast, stretching from Binalong Bay to Eddystone Point. The orange colour comes from lichen. Captain Tobias Furneaux named it in 1773 after the fires he saw Aboriginal people lighting on the beaches. The northern end lies in Mount William National Park, while the southern end is a conservation area, with St Helens the main base.

goodToKnow.title: Base in St Helens
goodToKnow.detail: St Helens is the largest coastal town in the region, about two hours' drive from Launceston, and the gateway to the Bay of Fires.

goodToKnow.title: A windswept coast
goodToKnow.detail: The coastline is windswept, so bring a windproof layer even on a sunny beach day.

name: Stanley
tagline: A village beneath a flat-topped volcanic plug on Bass Strait.
description: Stanley is a village of about 550 people in the north-west, best known for The Nut, a volcanic plug rising 143 m beside the sea and visible from almost everywhere in town. A chairlift and a steep zigzag track climb it, and a circuit on top looks over Bass Strait and Rocky Cape National Park. Highfield, a homestead from the Regency period just outside town, is open daily to visitors. Little penguins can be seen coming ashore just after dark.

goodToKnow.title: Car access only
goodToKnow.detail: The only way into Stanley is by car; it is a little over an hour from Burnie, so plan the drive in.

goodToKnow.title: Chairlift or zigzag track
goodToKnow.detail: Ride the chairlift up The Nut, or take the steeper Zig Zag Track, then walk the 4.6 km circuit on top (about an hour).

goodToKnow.title: Penguin etiquette
goodToKnow.detail: At the viewing area just after dark, do not use flash or a bright torch, which can harm the penguins' eyes; a red light is better.
